nebulae.name: Orion Nebula (M42)
nebulae.blurb: The nearest massive star-forming region to Earth, visible to the naked eye as the middle 'star' of Orion's sword. The four hot Trapezium stars at its core carve out and light the entire glowing cavity.

nebulae.name: Carina Nebula (NGC 3372)
nebulae.blurb: A southern giant several times larger than Orion, home to the erupting star Eta Carinae, which briefly became the second-brightest star in the sky during its 1840s Great Eruption. Its dust pillars and 'Mystic Mountain' are sculpted by dozens of O-type stars.

nebulae.name: Eagle Nebula (M16)
nebulae.blurb: Home of the Pillars of Creation, towers of cold gas and dust about 4-5 light-years tall made famous by Hubble in 1995. New stars are condensing inside the pillars even as ultraviolet light from nearby hot stars erodes them away.

nebulae.name: Lagoon Nebula (M8)
nebulae.blurb: A naked-eye stellar nursery in Sagittarius, split by the dark dust lane that gives it its name. At its heart lies the Hourglass Nebula, a tight knot of gas being blasted by the O-star Herschel 36.

nebulae.name: Trifid Nebula (M20)
nebulae.blurb: A rare three-in-one: a red emission nebula, a blue reflection nebula, and the dark dust lanes that trisect it and give it its name. It lies just north of the Lagoon Nebula in the star clouds of Sagittarius.

nebulae.name: Rosette Nebula (NGC 2237)
nebulae.blurb: A vast cosmic rose in Monoceros whose central hole was blown clear by winds from the young cluster NGC 2244 born inside it. On the sky it spans more than twice the diameter of the full Moon.

nebulae.name: Crab Nebula (M1)
nebulae.blurb: The shredded remains of a supernova that Chinese astronomers watched explode in 1054 AD, bright enough to be seen in daylight for weeks. Its central pulsar spins about 30 times per second, energizing the nebula's eerie blue synchrotron glow.

nebulae.name: Ring Nebula (M57)
nebulae.blurb: The archetypal planetary nebula in Lyra: a barrel of glowing gas about one light-year across, cast off by a dying Sun-like star whose white-dwarf remnant still shines at its center. JWST imaging in 2023 revealed some 20,000 dense knots of hydrogen in its ring.

nebulae.name: Helix Nebula (NGC 7293)
nebulae.blurb: One of the closest planetary nebulae to Earth, nicknamed the 'Eye of God' for its cyan pupil and red rim. Thousands of comet-like knots, each larger than our solar system, stream away from its central white dwarf.

nebulae.name: Dumbbell Nebula (M27)
nebulae.blurb: The first planetary nebula ever discovered, found by Charles Messier in 1764. Its two bright lobes are an hourglass of expelled stellar atmosphere seen from the side, still expanding after roughly 10,000 years.

nebulae.name: Cat's Eye Nebula (NGC 6543)
nebulae.blurb: An intricately layered planetary nebula in Draco whose dying star shed at least eleven concentric shells at intervals of roughly 1,500 years. It was the first planetary nebula ever studied with a spectroscope, by William Huggins in 1864.

nebulae.name: Veil Nebula (Cygnus Loop)
nebulae.blurb: Delicate red and teal filaments tracing the shockwave of a star that exploded 10,000 to 20,000 years ago. The full loop spans about three degrees of sky, the width of six full Moons side by side.

nebulae.name: North America Nebula (NGC 7000)
nebulae.blurb: A glowing continent in Cygnus whose 'Gulf of Mexico' is carved by a foreground dust cloud. The hot star that ionizes it, the Bajamar Star, hides behind that dust and was only pinned down in the Gaia era.

nebulae.name: Horsehead Nebula (Barnard 33)
nebulae.blurb: The sky's most famous dark nebula: a chess-knight silhouette of cold dust about 3.5 light-years tall, backlit by the red glow of emission nebula IC 434. The ultraviolet glare of nearby Sigma Orionis is slowly evaporating it.

nebulae.name: Flame Nebula (NGC 2024)
nebulae.blurb: A fiery tangle of glowing gas and dark dust lanes right beside Alnitak, the easternmost star of Orion's Belt, whose ultraviolet light sets it aglow. Infrared views reveal a dense cluster of newborn stars hidden inside its dusty core.

nebulae.name: Omega Nebula (M17)
nebulae.blurb: Also called the Swan Nebula for its checkmark shape, this Sagittarius nursery is one of the most massive star-forming regions in the Milky Way. Its hidden central cluster holds hundreds of young stars veiled by dust.

nebulae.name: Butterfly Nebula (NGC 6302)
nebulae.blurb: A bipolar planetary nebula whose wings of roiling gas span over three light-years, heated to more than 20,000 degrees. Its buried central star burns at roughly 250,000 K, making it one of the hottest stars known.

nebulae.name: Pelican Nebula (IC 5070)
nebulae.blurb: The North America Nebula's neighbor across a dark dust channel, shaped like a pelican in profile. Its ionization front is actively advancing into cold gas, sprouting dark tendrils tipped with newborn stars and Herbig-Haro jets.

nebulae.name: Heart Nebula (IC 1805)
nebulae.blurb: A vast valentine of glowing hydrogen in Cassiopeia, sculpted by winds and radiation from the young cluster Melotte 15 at its center, whose stars include some nearly 50 times the Sun's mass. It forms a famous pair with the neighboring Soul Nebula.

nebulae.name: California Nebula (NGC 1499)
nebulae.blurb: A drifting streak of hydrogen in Perseus that uncannily matches the outline of the US state of California, stretching about 2.5 degrees across the sky. It glows red under the ultraviolet light of the hot runaway star Xi Persei (Menkib).

nebulae.name: Tarantula Nebula (30 Doradus)
nebulae.blurb: The most luminous star-forming region in the entire Local Group, blazing in the Large Magellanic Cloud around the super star cluster R136, home to the most massive stars known. If it sat as close as the Orion Nebula, it would cast shadows on Earth.

nebulae.name: Iris Nebula (NGC 7023)
nebulae.blurb: A luminous blue flower in Cepheus, six light-years across, whose petals are dust grains reflecting the light of the young star HD 200775. Its dusty filaments faintly fluoresce red with polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons.

nebulae.name: Witch Head Nebula (IC 2118)
nebulae.blurb: A cackling witch's profile in Eridanus, glowing ghostly blue with light reflected from brilliant Rigel a couple of degrees away. Its fine dust scatters blue light more efficiently than red, the same physics that colors Earth's sky.

nebulae.name: Bubble Nebula (NGC 7635)
nebulae.blurb: A near-perfect soap bubble seven light-years across, inflated by the ferocious stellar wind of the massive star BD+60 2522, which sits off-center inside its own creation. Hubble made it the showpiece of its 26th-anniversary image in 2016.

exoplanets.name: Proxima Centauri
exoplanets.blurb: The closest star to the Sun hosts Proxima b, a roughly Earth-mass planet orbiting inside the habitable zone just 4.2 light-years away. Its 2016 discovery made the nearest star system also the nearest known exoplanet system.

planets.name: Proxima b
planets.note: Habitable-zone world; min mass 1.07 Earth masses; radius estimated (non-transiting)

planets.name: Proxima d
planets.note: Sub-Earth, min mass 0.26 Earth masses; radius estimated

planets.name: Proxima c
planets.note: Cold super-Earth candidate (~7 Earth masses); existence still debated

exoplanets.name: TRAPPIST-1
exoplanets.blurb: An ultracool dwarf barely larger than Jupiter with seven transiting Earth-sized planets, three to four of them in or near the habitable zone. The whole system would fit inside Mercury's orbit, its planets locked in a resonant chain.

planets.name: TRAPPIST-1 b
planets.note: Innermost; JWST finds little or no atmosphere

planets.name: TRAPPIST-1 c
planets.note: Venus-like irradiation

planets.name: TRAPPIST-1 d
planets.note: Smallest of the seven

planets.name: TRAPPIST-1 e
planets.note: Best habitable-zone candidate of the system

planets.name: TRAPPIST-1 f
planets.note: Habitable zone; likely volatile-rich

planets.name: TRAPPIST-1 g
planets.note: Habitable-zone outer edge

planets.name: TRAPPIST-1 h
planets.note: Outermost and coldest

exoplanets.name: 51 Pegasi
exoplanets.blurb: In 1995 Mayor and Queloz found 51 Pegasi b here, the first exoplanet ever discovered around a Sun-like star, a feat honored with the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics. Its scorching 4.2-day orbit invented the whole category of hot Jupiters.

planets.name: 51 Pegasi b (Dimidium)
planets.note: First exoplanet around a Sun-like star; min mass 0.46 Jupiter masses; radius estimated (non-transiting hot Jupiter)

exoplanets.name: Tau Ceti
exoplanets.blurb: The nearest single Sun-like star, a fixture of SETI searches and science fiction, shows radial-velocity signals of four super-Earth candidates, two of them near the habitable zone. It also hosts a massive debris disk, making it a scaled-up analog of the young Solar System.

planets.name: Tau Ceti g
planets.note: RV candidate, min mass ~1.75 Earth masses; radius estimated

planets.name: Tau Ceti h
planets.note: RV candidate, min mass ~1.8 Earth masses; radius estimated

planets.name: Tau Ceti e
planets.note: RV candidate near inner habitable-zone edge; min mass ~3.9 Earth masses; radius estimated

planets.name: Tau Ceti f
planets.note: RV candidate in the habitable zone; min mass ~3.9 Earth masses; radius estimated

exoplanets.name: Epsilon Eridani
exoplanets.blurb: A young, nearby orange dwarf ringed by asteroid belts and a cold debris disk, with a Jupiter-like planet, AEgir, confirmed on a 7.4-year orbit. At only 10.5 light-years it is one of our best windows onto a planetary system still settling down.

planets.name: Epsilon Eridani b (AEgir)
planets.note: Jupiter analog, ~0.7-0.8 Jupiter masses; radius estimated (not transiting); system also hosts debris belts

exoplanets.name: Kepler-90
exoplanets.blurb: The first star known to host eight planets, tying the Solar System's count, arranged like a compressed copy of our own with small worlds inside and giants outside. The eighth planet, Kepler-90i, was found in 2017 by a Google neural network mining Kepler data.

planets.name: Kepler-90 b
planets.note: Hot super-Earth

planets.name: Kepler-90 c
planets.note: Hot super-Earth

planets.name: Kepler-90 i
planets.note: Found by machine learning (2017); the eighth planet

planets.name: Kepler-90 d
planets.note: Sub-Neptune

planets.name: Kepler-90 e
planets.note: Sub-Neptune

planets.name: Kepler-90 f
planets.note: Sub-Neptune

planets.name: Kepler-90 g
planets.note: Gas giant

planets.name: Kepler-90 h
planets.note: Jupiter-sized, at an Earth-like distance

exoplanets.name: Kepler-452
exoplanets.blurb: Home of Kepler-452b, announced in 2015 as "Earth's older, bigger cousin": a super-Earth in a 385-day orbit within the habitable zone of a G2 star much like the Sun, but 1.5 billion years older. It remains an icon of the search for Earth 2.0.

planets.name: Kepler-452b
planets.note: Habitable-zone super-Earth around a Sun-like star; 'Earth's cousin'

exoplanets.name: HD 209458
exoplanets.blurb: Its hot Jupiter, nicknamed Osiris, was the first exoplanet seen transiting its star (1999) and the first with a detected atmosphere, including a comet-like tail of escaping hydrogen. It launched transit science, now the dominant way exoplanets are found and characterized.

planets.name: HD 209458 b (Osiris)
planets.note: First transiting exoplanet; first exoplanet atmosphere detection; evaporating hydrogen envelope

exoplanets.name: HD 189733
exoplanets.blurb: Hosts the best-studied hot Jupiter in the sky, whose true color was measured as deep cobalt blue, likely from silicate-glass clouds whipped by 8,000 km/h winds where it may rain molten glass sideways. Water, sodium, and carbon dioxide have all been detected in its atmosphere.

planets.name: HD 189733 b
planets.note: Cobalt-blue hot Jupiter; benchmark for exoplanet atmosphere studies

exoplanets.name: 55 Cancri
exoplanets.blurb: A naked-eye Sun-like star (with a distant red-dwarf companion) hosting five known planets, one of the first rich multi-planet systems. Its transiting super-Earth 55 Cancri e is a lava world with a possible mineral atmosphere, orbiting in under 18 hours.

planets.name: 55 Cancri e (Janssen)
planets.note: Ultra-short-period lava super-Earth, ~8 Earth masses; JWST target

planets.name: 55 Cancri b (Galileo)
planets.note: Warm giant, min mass ~0.8 Jupiter masses; radius estimated

planets.name: 55 Cancri c (Brahe)
planets.note: Saturn-mass planet (~0.17 Jupiter masses); radius estimated

planets.name: 55 Cancri f (Harriot)
planets.note: Sub-Saturn near the habitable zone; radius estimated

planets.name: 55 Cancri d (Lipperhey)
planets.note: Outer Jupiter analog, min mass ~3-4 Jupiter masses; radius estimated

exoplanets.name: Gliese 876
exoplanets.blurb: In 1998 this nearby red dwarf yielded the first planet ever found around an M dwarf, and it later revealed one of the first known super-Earths. Three of its four planets are locked in a striking 1:2:4 Laplace resonance, like Jupiter's moons Io, Europa, and Ganymede.

planets.name: Gliese 876 d
planets.note: One of the first super-Earths (2005), ~6.8 Earth masses; radius estimated

planets.name: Gliese 876 c
planets.note: Giant, ~0.71 Jupiter masses; in 1:2:4 resonance; radius estimated

planets.name: Gliese 876 b
planets.note: First planet found around an M dwarf (1998), ~2.3 Jupiter masses; radius estimated

planets.name: Gliese 876 e
planets.note: Neptune-mass (~15 Earth masses), completes the Laplace resonance chain; radius estimated

exoplanets.name: K2-18
exoplanets.blurb: Its habitable-zone sub-Neptune K2-18 b became the first habitable-zone planet with water vapor reported in its atmosphere (2019), and JWST later found methane and carbon dioxide consistent with a possible ocean-covered 'Hycean' world. Claims of the biosignature gas DMS remain hotly debated.

planets.name: K2-18 b
planets.note: Habitable-zone sub-Neptune, ~8.6 Earth masses; candidate Hycean world; disputed DMS detection

planets.name: K2-18 c
planets.note: Non-transiting RV candidate, min mass ~5.6 Earth masses; existence debated

exoplanets.name: TOI-700
exoplanets.blurb: TESS's first Earth-sized habitable-zone discovery: this quiet red dwarf hosts two roughly Earth-sized worlds, TOI-700 d and e, in or near its habitable zone. Its low flare activity makes it one of the most promising nearby systems for temperate small planets.

planets.name: TOI-700 b
planets.note: Earth-sized inner planet

planets.name: TOI-700 c
planets.note: Sub-Neptune

planets.name: TOI-700 e
planets.note: Earth-sized, in the optimistic habitable zone (found 2023)

planets.name: TOI-700 d
planets.note: TESS's first Earth-sized habitable-zone planet (2020)

exoplanets.name: Fomalhaut
exoplanets.blurb: A brilliant young A-type star encircled by a sharp-edged debris ring orbiting about 136 AU from the star; the point of light imaged inside it in 2008, hailed as the first directly photographed exoplanet, later faded and expanded, revealing itself as an expanding dust cloud from a colossal planetesimal collision. JWST has since mapped nested inner belts hinting at unseen planets.

extra.disk: Eccentric debris ring at ~136 AU imaged by Hubble; JWST (2023) revealed inner asteroid belt and intermediate belt, suggesting hidden shepherding planets

planets.name: Fomalhaut b (Dagon)
planets.note: Imaged by Hubble in 2008 as the 'first directly imaged exoplanet'; faded and expanded by 2020, now interpreted as a dispersing dust cloud from a planetesimal collision on a belt-crossing orbit

blackholes.name: Cygnus X-1
blackholes.blurb: The first object widely accepted as a black hole, and the subject of Stephen Hawking's famous lost bet with Kip Thorne. It devours a stream of gas torn from its blue supergiant companion, blazing in X-rays.

extra.discovered: 1964 (X-ray rocket survey); accepted as a black hole in the 1970s-90s

blackholes.name: V404 Cygni
blackholes.blurb: A sleeping monster that erupts spectacularly: its June 2015 outburst briefly made it the brightest X-ray source in the sky, flickering so violently it was visible to modest amateur telescopes.

blackholes.name: A0620-00 (V616 Mon)
blackholes.blurb: Discovered as the brightest X-ray nova ever seen in 1975, this quiet system held the title of closest known black hole to Earth for over four decades until Gaia BH1 dethroned it.

blackholes.name: Gaia BH1
blackholes.blurb: The closest known black hole to Earth, found in 2022 not by any glow of its own but by the telltale wobble it imposes on a Sun-like star orbiting it — a truly dormant black hole hiding in plain sight.

blackholes.name: GRS 1915+105
blackholes.blurb: The prototype microquasar: in 1994 its radio jets appeared to blast outward faster than light — an illusion of relativistic motion — the first superluminal source ever seen inside our own Galaxy.

blackholes.name: M87*
blackholes.blurb: The first black hole ever photographed: the Event Horizon Telescope's 2019 image of its glowing orange ring made history. It anchors galaxy M87 and launches a plasma jet 5,000 light-years long.

blackholes.name: 3C 273
blackholes.blurb: The first quasar ever identified: Maarten Schmidt's 1963 redshift measurement revealed a starlike dot was actually a blazing galactic nucleus billions of light-years away — the optically brightest quasar in our sky.

blackholes.name: TON 618
blackholes.blurb: Home to one of the most massive black holes known, roughly 66 billion solar masses — an 'ultramassive' black hole whose event horizon would swallow a dozen Solar Systems laid end to end, shining with the light of trillions of Suns.

extra.discovered: 1957 (Tonantzintla survey); identified as a quasar in 1970

galaxies.name: M81 (Bode's Galaxy)
galaxies.blurb: A textbook grand-design spiral and the gravitational anchor of the M81 Group, locked in a slow tidal dance with its neighbors M82 and NGC 3077. Its nucleus harbors a 70-million-solar-mass black hole, and it is bright enough to glimpse in binoculars.
galaxies.color: warm yellow core with blue spiral arms

galaxies.name: M82 (Cigar Galaxy)
galaxies.blurb: The prototype starburst galaxy: a close pass by M81 ignited star formation roughly ten times the Milky Way's rate, driving a glowing bipolar wind of hydrogen thousands of light-years out of its edge-on disk. Supernovae pop off here every decade or so.
galaxies.color: red hydrogen-alpha outflow piercing a pale edge-on disk

galaxies.name: M51 (Whirlpool Galaxy)
galaxies.blurb: The first galaxy ever seen to have spiral structure, sketched by Lord Rosse in 1845. Its perfect face-on arms are being wound up and lit with star formation by the ongoing pull of its yellow companion NGC 5195, connected by a visible tidal bridge.
galaxies.color: blue star-forming arms laced with pink HII regions

galaxies.name: M101 (Pinwheel Galaxy)
galaxies.blurb: A giant face-on spiral nearly twice the Milky Way's diameter, holding perhaps a trillion stars and some 3,000 cataloged star-forming regions. Its lopsided arms betray gravitational nudges from companion galaxies; supernova SN 2011fe flared here in 2011.
galaxies.color: blue asymmetric arms, faint yellow core

galaxies.name: M104 (Sombrero Galaxy)
galaxies.blurb: Tilted just six degrees from edge-on, its brilliant bulge and sharp dust lane form the unmistakable hat-brim silhouette. It blends a spiral's disk with an elliptical-like halo of some 2,000 globular clusters and hosts a billion-solar-mass central black hole.
galaxies.color: glowing white bulge bisected by a dark dust lane

galaxies.name: Centaurus A (NGC 5128)
galaxies.blurb: The nearest active radio galaxy: an elliptical wrapped in a warped dust lane, the wreckage of a swallowed spiral. Its central supermassive black hole fires relativistic jets that inflate radio lobes spanning over a million light-years of sky.
galaxies.color: golden elliptical glow crossed by a dark twisted dust band

galaxies.name: NGC 253 (Sculptor Galaxy)
galaxies.blurb: The dominant galaxy of the Sculptor Group and one of the dustiest, most vigorously star-forming spirals in our neighborhood, discovered by Caroline Herschel in 1783. Seen at a steep 78-degree tilt, its mottled disk hides a nuclear starburst driving a hot galactic wind.
galaxies.color: dusty amber disk with silvery star clouds

galaxies.name: M83 (Southern Pinwheel)
galaxies.blurb: A luminous face-on barred spiral crackling with star formation along its arms and central bar. It is one of the most prolific supernova factories known, with six recorded in the last century, and shines as the southern sky's answer to M101.
galaxies.color: pink starbirth knots along vivid blue arms

galaxies.name: M94 (Croc's Eye Galaxy)
galaxies.blurb: A ringed spiral whose inner disk is encircled by a brilliant band of newborn stars, giving it a striking eye-like appearance. Studies suggest it contains unusually little dark matter, making it a puzzle for galaxy-formation models.
galaxies.color: bright yellow core ringed by a blue starburst annulus

extra.type: SA(r)ab ringed spiral with starburst ring

galaxies.name: M63 (Sunflower Galaxy)
galaxies.blurb: The archetypal flocculent spiral: instead of two sweeping arms, its disk is covered in short, patchy tufts of star formation like sunflower petals. A faint giant stellar stream loops around it, the remains of a shredded dwarf companion.
galaxies.color: mottled blue-white petals around an amber center

galaxies.name: NGC 4565 (Needle Galaxy)
galaxies.blurb: The finest edge-on spiral in the northern sky: a razor-thin luminous disk split by a knife-edge dust lane, with a boxy peanut-shaped bulge betraying a central bar. It is likely what the Milky Way would look like viewed exactly from the side.
galaxies.color: pale silver needle split by a thin dark dust lane

galaxies.name: M49
galaxies.blurb: The optically brightest member of the Virgo Cluster and the first cluster galaxy ever discovered, found by Messier in 1771. This giant elliptical holds several thousand globular clusters and is quietly cannibalizing the dwarf galaxy UGC 7636.
galaxies.color: smooth yellow-white elliptical glow

galaxies.name: M87 (Virgo A)
galaxies.blurb: The supergiant elliptical at the Virgo Cluster's heart, cloaked in roughly 15,000 globular clusters and firing a 5,000-light-year relativistic jet. Its central black hole M87*, 6.5 billion solar masses, became the first ever photographed by the Event Horizon Telescope in 2019.
galaxies.color: smooth golden halo with a blue synchrotron jet

galaxies.name: M60
galaxies.blurb: A giant elliptical on the eastern edge of the Virgo Cluster, hosting a 4.5-billion-solar-mass black hole. It makes a famous odd couple with the overlapping spiral NGC 4647, and its ultracompact dwarf satellite M60-UCD1 is one of the densest galaxies known.
galaxies.color: creamy yellow elliptical paired with a faint blue spiral

galaxies.name: NGC 4038/4039 (Antennae Galaxies)
galaxies.blurb: The nearest and most famous major galaxy merger, two spirals that began colliding a few hundred million years ago. The crash has flung two curving tidal tails of stars roughly half a million light-years long and spawned thousands of young super star clusters.
galaxies.color: twin golden cores in blue chaos with long faint tails

galaxies.name: M74 (Phantom Galaxy)
galaxies.blurb: A perfectly face-on grand-design spiral so diffuse that visual observers call it the Phantom, yet JWST images reveal its two arms as crisp lanes of gas and dust threaded with star clusters. It is a favorite laboratory for studying spiral density waves.
galaxies.color: ghostly blue symmetric arms, faint yellow nucleus

galaxies.name: M77 (Cetus A)
galaxies.blurb: The archetype of Seyfert galaxies: its compact nucleus blazes with radiation from an actively feeding supermassive black hole hidden behind a torus of dust. One of the largest and most luminous Messier galaxies, it anchors its own small group in Cetus.
galaxies.color: intense white active nucleus in tightly wound arms

galaxies.name: NGC 2903
galaxies.blurb: A bright barred spiral in Leo that Messier somehow missed, famous among amateur astronomers as the best non-Messier galaxy in the northern sky. Its central bar funnels gas into a hotspot-studded nuclear ring of furious star formation.
galaxies.color: yellow bar with knotty blue arms

galaxies.name: M106
galaxies.blurb: A Seyfert spiral famous for its anomalous extra arms, glowing streams of gas shocked by jets from its central black hole rather than made of stars. Water megamasers orbiting that black hole yield one of astronomy's most precise direct distance measurements.
galaxies.color: red anomalous arms over a blue-white tilted disk

extra.type: SAB(s)bc Seyfert spiral with anomalous arms

galaxies.name: NGC 891
galaxies.blurb: A Milky Way twin seen exactly edge-on in Andromeda, its dark equatorial dust lane frayed by vertical filaments of gas blown out of the disk by supernovae. Long a favorite of astrophotographers, it is one of the brightest members of the small NGC 1023 Group.
galaxies.color: warm stellar disk cut by a ragged dark dust lane

clusters.name: Pleiades (M45)
clusters.blurb: The Seven Sisters: a young cluster of hot blue stars about 100 million years old, drifting through a chance cloud of interstellar dust that scatters their light into wispy blue veils. Gaia counts over a thousand members, most too faint for the naked eye.

clusters.name: Hyades
clusters.blurb: The nearest open cluster to the Sun, forming the V-shaped face of Taurus the Bull (bright orange Aldebaran is a foreground interloper). Its roughly 700 members, about 650 million years old, share a common motion and are slowly evaporating into tidal tails.

clusters.name: Double Cluster (h + χ Persei)
clusters.blurb: Twin clusters NGC 869 and NGC 884, born together about 13 million years ago and physically neighbors in the Perseus spiral arm. Each holds thousands of stars, including brilliant blue supergiants sprinkled with contrasting ruby-red supergiants.

clusters.name: Beehive Cluster (M44)
clusters.blurb: Known since antiquity as Praesepe, the Manger, a naked-eye smudge that Galileo's telescope first resolved into a swarm of stars. About 600-700 million years old with roughly a thousand members, it shares an age and motion with the Hyades, hinting at a common birth cloud. Several of its stars host known exoplanets.

clusters.name: Wild Duck Cluster (M11)
clusters.blurb: One of the richest and most compact open clusters known, with nearly 3,000 stars packed so tightly it almost resembles a loose globular. Its brightest members trace a rough triangle that 19th-century observers likened to a flight of wild ducks.

clusters.name: Jewel Box (NGC 4755)
clusters.blurb: John Herschel likened this southern cluster to a casket of variously colored precious stones: sapphire-blue supergiants set against a striking ruby-red supergiant. At roughly 14 million years old it is one of the youngest clusters known, anchored by the star Kappa Crucis near the Southern Cross.

clusters.name: M67
clusters.blurb: One of the oldest open clusters known, about 4 billion years old — most clusters dissolve long before this age. Its stars closely match the Sun's age and chemistry, making it a benchmark laboratory for stellar evolution and a long-debated candidate birthplace for solar siblings.

clusters.name: Omega Centauri (NGC 5139)
clusters.blurb: The most massive globular cluster of the Milky Way: roughly 10 million stars whose multiple ages and chemistries suggest it may be the stripped core of a dwarf galaxy the Milky Way devoured. Stars in its center sit only about 0.1 light-year apart, and its heart may harbor an intermediate-mass black hole.

clusters.name: 47 Tucanae (NGC 104)
clusters.blurb: The second-brightest globular in the sky, a blazing ball of roughly a million ancient stars near the Small Magellanic Cloud (a chance alignment). Its dense core is a factory of exotica: dozens of millisecond pulsars and blue stragglers forged in stellar collisions.

clusters.name: Hercules Cluster (M13)
clusters.blurb: The great globular of the northern sky, several hundred thousand stars about 12 billion years old. In 1974 the Arecibo radio telescope beamed humanity's most famous interstellar message toward it — a signal that will take over 22,000 years to arrive.

clusters.name: M22
clusters.blurb: One of the nearest and brightest globular clusters, seen through the rich star fields toward the galactic center in Sagittarius. It was among the first globulars ever discovered (1665) and hosts two stellar-mass black hole candidates plus a rare planetary nebula.

clusters.name: M4
clusters.blurb: The closest globular cluster to Earth, hanging beside red Antares in Scorpius. It contains some of the oldest white dwarfs known and the pulsar planet PSR B1620-26 b, nicknamed Methuselah — a world nearly as old as the universe itself.

clusters.name: M15
clusters.blurb: One of the oldest and densest globulars known, roughly 12-13 billion years old, whose center has undergone core collapse — stars crowding into an extraordinarily compact central cusp. It also hosts Pease 1, the first planetary nebula ever found inside a globular cluster.

clusters.name: R136
clusters.blurb: The ferocious young super star cluster at the heart of the Tarantula Nebula in the Large Magellanic Cloud, only about 1-2 million years old. Its compact core concentrates the most massive stars known, including R136a1 at roughly 200 solar masses, whose combined winds and ultraviolet light carve the surrounding nebula.

clusters.name: Mayall II (G1)
clusters.blurb: The brightest globular cluster in the entire Local Group, orbiting the Andromeda Galaxy some 130,000 light-years from its center. Hubble resolved at least 300,000 ancient stars in it, and its mass — roughly twice Omega Centauri's — plus its spread of stellar chemistries suggest it too may be a cannibalized dwarf galaxy's core.
